title: Resolving Construction Contract Disputes 2026: Mediation, Arbitration, Court
desc: How construction contract disputes are resolved: negotiation, mediation, arbitration, courts, dispute boards; limitation periods and continuing the work.
summary: Ways to resolve disputes between homeowners and contractors under the Construction Law 2025, Decree 210/2026/ND-CP and the Civil Code, with notes on limitation periods.
body: Delays, extra costs, and poor quality are common causes of disagreement between homeowners and contractors. This article summarizes the ways the law allows disputes to be resolved under Article 86 of the Construction Law 2025, Article 17 of Decree 210/2026/ND-CP, and the Civil Code.
Under Clause 5, Article 86 of the Construction Law, construction contract disputes are handled through:
A dispute-handling model following international practice (a dispute board);

Which method is used is for the parties to agree (Clause 1, Article 17 of Decree 210). The contract should therefore include a dispute resolution clause stating clearly: how long to negotiate, where mediation takes place, and then whether to go to arbitration or court.

When one party finds the other is not performing in line with the contract, it has the right to make a complaint demanding proper performance; the party complained against must give specific grounds and evidence (Article 21 of Decree 210). The complaint must be sent to the agreed address for dealings. For public investment and PPP projects, the party receiving the complaint must reply in writing within at most 7 days. A complaint that cannot be resolved moves on to dispute resolution.
All proposals and requests during contract performance should be made in writing (Clause 4, Article 4); this is important evidence if the matter goes to arbitration or court.
3. Work must continue during a dispute

While a dispute is being resolved, the parties must continue performing the work that is not affected by the disputed matter and must not interrupt the contract, except for force majeure, a request from a competent authority, or a case where suspension is permitted by regulation (Clause 2, Article 17). Stopping work without authority can turn you into the party in breach.

The parties may agree to set up a dispute board right after signing the contract or when a dispute arises; its members must be objective, independent, and free of conflicts of interest. The cost of the board is borne half by each party, unless otherwise agreed (Clause 3, Article 17). This model is often used for large projects.
Bonuses, penalties for breach, and compensation for damage must be agreed by the parties in the contract (Clause 1, Article 86).
Compensation is determined by actual damage, or by pre-agreed damages corresponding to the obligation breached and the degree of breach (Clause 2).
For public investment and PPP projects, the penalty may not exceed 12% of the value of the part of the contract that was breached (Clause 3).
If the breach is caused by a third party (for example, a supplier), the breaching party remains responsible to the other party (Clause 4).

The limitation period for asking a court to resolve a contract dispute is 3 years from the date the person entitled to make a claim knew or should have known that their rights were infringed (Article 429 of the Civil Code). For commercial disputes under the Commercial Law (usually between businesses), the limitation period is two years (Article 319 of the Commercial Law). Do not wait until the deadline has passed to sue.

This article is a summary for reference only and does not replace legal documents. Procedures before arbitration and courts follow procedural and arbitration law (not yet in our library). The Commercial Law 2005 is partially no longer in force. For disputes of large value, it is advisable to consult a lawyer.
